judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 493. It bars people finally convicted of a first- or second-degree felony from serving as poll watchers. Texas already barred people with an election-related felony, and appointees must now swear in writing that they have no covered conviction. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 86-52.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against House Bill 493. It bars people finally convicted of a first- or second-degree felony from serving as poll watchers. judgments.yea_description: Voted to approve the final, negotiated version of House Bill 493 in the Texas Senate. The law bars anyone finally convicted of a first- or second-degree felony from serving as a poll watcher. Those are the two most serious felony levels. A poll watcher is a person a party or candidate sends to observe voting. Texas already barred people convicted of an election-related felony. Appointees must now swear in writing that they have no such conviction. The Senate adopted the report 23-8 and the law took effect September 1, 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 521. Curbside voters must swear they cannot enter without help or need help because of a disability, and someone escorting such a voter may also get a curbside ballot. When at least four poll workers are present, two must carry the ballot; campaigning is barred within 20 feet; and knowingly skipping the form after driving seven or more voters is a Class A misdemeanor, the state's most serious minor crime. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 84-54.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 5115. It raises the election fraud listed in state Election Code Section 276.013 from the most serious misdemeanor to a second-degree felony, makes it a first-degree felony for elected officials, and makes an attempt a third-degree felony. It also covers knowingly counting an invalid vote or refusing to count a valid one. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 88-54.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 510. It lets the secretary of state withhold voter-registration money from a county official after written notice and a fair chance to fix late or missing work. Covered duties include handling registrations, registration challenges, and address-check notices on time. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 109-33.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1362. It bars Texas offices from using red flag orders unless state law allows them; these court orders take guns from people judged dangerous for a time. Offices cannot take federal money to enforce them; using an order not issued under Texas law becomes the lowest felony level, while current family and crime-related protection orders stay. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 86-53.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 2284, which limits local bow and gun rules. It extends the state ban on city and county firearm rules to archery equipment, so local governments may no longer regulate bows, crossbows, or arrows. It also drops firearms from a municipal fire-prevention power and changes the county bow-hunting lot limit from 10 acres or less to smaller than seven acres. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 96-43.

judgments.yea_description: Voted through Senate Bill 11 to let school boards create a daily school prayer and religious-reading period. Participants must give up legal claims that the prayer time breaks church-state rules; the time cannot use the school speaker system; and the state must defend participating schools. It also removes the rule against urging students to pray or not pray. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 88-48.

A government office may limit it only to serve a vital public goal and must use the narrowest rule that works. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 86-48.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1257 in the Texas House, the last vote before it went to the governor. Health plans that cover a gender transition procedure must also cover its side effects and any reversal. That includes yearly monitoring, and care for people who joined the plan after the procedure. Plans that large employers pay for themselves are not covered. The House passed it 87-58 and the law took effect September 1, 2025.

Plans that large employers pay for themselves are not covered. The House passed it 87-58 and the law took effect September 1, 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 1257. Health plans that cover or once covered a patient's gender transition procedure must also cover side effects, yearly checks, and care to manage or reverse it. Coverage applies even if the patient joined the plan later, while employer plans that pay claims themselves are exempt. The bill became law after the Texas Senate passed it 20-11.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass House Bill 3441. It lets people harmed by a vaccine sue its maker for direct losses, court costs, and lawyer fees if the maker paid to advertise it in Texas. They have three years to sue, while doctor-patient talks and materials shown in a clinic do not count as ads. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 88-31.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass the House version of Senate Bill 379. That version barred food aid from buying fizzy soft drinks with at least five grams of added sugar or any artificial sweetener. Milk products and drinks mostly made of fruit or vegetable juice were exempt. The House passed it 90-37 before a later House-Senate deal became law and also covered sweetened drinks without bubbles and candy.

The House passed it 90-37 before a later House-Senate deal became law and also covered sweetened drinks without bubbles and candy.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass the Senate version of Senate Bill 379. That version barred food aid from buying energy drinks, sweetened or fizzy drinks, candy, chips, and cookies. Milk products and unsweetened fruit or vegetable juice were exempt. The Senate passed it 22-8 before a later House-Senate deal became law and narrowed the ban to sweetened drinks and candy.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 2337. Businesses that tell shareholders how to vote must tell the client, company, and public when advice uses goals not tied to money, such as environmental or diversity goals. If they give very different advice to clients who did not ask for it, they must tell those clients, the company, and the attorney general, and harmed people may sue. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 92-50.

The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 92-50.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass Senate Bill 21. It created the Texas Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, a special fund outside the state treasury held and managed by the comptroller. The reserve may buy only bitcoin or other cryptocurrency whose average market value over the past 24 months was at least $500 billion. The comptroller must report to the legislature every two years, advised by a five-member committee. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 101-42.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against Senate Bill 21. It created the Texas Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, a special fund outside the state treasury held and managed by the comptroller. The reserve may buy only bitcoin or other cryptocurrency whose average market value over the past 24 months was at least $500 billion. The comptroller must report to the legislature every two years, advised by a five-member committee. The bill became law after the Texas House passed it 101-42.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the final House-Senate deal on Senate Bill 21. It created the Texas Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, a fund outside the state treasury run by the comptroller. Any bitcoin or other cryptocurrency bought with reserve money must have averaged at least $500 billion in market value over the most recent 24 months. The comptroller must report to the legislature every two years, with advice from a new committee. The bill became law after the Texas Senate approved the compromise 23-8.
